routes.description: Establish resurrection as a plausible cumulative explanation of the early appearances, unexpected resurrection belief, subsequent Christian expansion, and continuing visions.
routes.successCriteria: Show that the historical lines jointly fit Jesus's resurrection and continuing agency more specifically than the proposed ordinary or comparative explanations.

motionBridge.description: The combined historical lines must make Jesus's resurrection a plausible explanation of the motion's specified phenomena.

centralBridges.description: Early individual and group appearance traditions must provide positive evidence that Jesus was encountered alive after death.
The immediate claim of an individually resurrected Messiah must require explanation beyond available Jewish postmortem categories.
Christianity's expansion must connect specifically to the mission and continuing agency attributed to the risen Jesus.
Later cross-cultural Jesus visions must constitute an additional phenomenon consistent with his continuing activity.

subsidiaryBridges.description: No single evidential line must bear the entire case; the lines must retain cumulative relevance when considered together.
Christian appearance and vision reports must be distinguishable from proposed parallels by their attestation, unexpectedness, or cross-cultural pattern.

routes.description: Account for the appearance beliefs, resurrection interpretation, Christian expansion, and later visions without treating a physical resurrection as the probable historical explanation.
routes.successCriteria: Show that source limitations, ordinary experiential mechanisms, cultural interpretation, religious growth, and comparative cases block the resurrection inference.

motionBridge.description: The available historical evidence must remain insufficient to prefer a unique physical resurrection over ordinary or historically comparable explanations.

centralBridges.description: The appearance evidence must be constrained by indirect testimony, sparse descriptions, and uncertainty about the reported witnesses.
Experiences and apocalyptic Jewish beliefs must supply a nonresurrection route to sincere claims that Jesus had been raised.
Religious expansion and fulfilled-mission claims must not establish what happened physically to Jesus's body.
Later Jesus dreams and visions must remain explainable through phenomena also reported in other religious traditions.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Historical inference must compare probabilities without assuming either that miracles are impossible or that testimony establishes them.
Standards applied to Christian testimony must also be applied to Mormon, Marian, and ancient appearance traditions.

sectionSelections.title: Early appearance testimony and comparative attestation
sectionSelections.rationale: The quality, number, and comparative force of the earliest reported witnesses form the principal evidential link between postmortem experiences and resurrection.

proSelections.proposition: Reports concerning Paul, Peter, James, Mary Magdalene, groups of disciples, and the five hundred form an early witness tradition offered as positive evidence of Jesus's resurrection.
Christian appearance testimony is presented as stronger than Islamic or Mormon miracle claims because it involves multiple accepted witnesses rather than one founding visionary.

conSelections.proposition: Only Paul directly attests his own experience, while claims concerning Peter, James, Mary, and the five hundred depend on indirect testimony and require comparison with other religions.
Mormon testimony concerning Moroni is presented as at least as directly documented and multiply attested as much New Testament appearance testimony, requiring consistent historical treatment.

sectionSelections.title: Unexpected messianic claim and Jewish interpretive categories
sectionSelections.rationale: The origin of belief in an already resurrected Messiah determines whether the claim itself points beyond ordinary experience or follows from available cultural interpretation.

proSelections.proposition: Paul, Peter, and Mary were not expecting Jesus or a crucified Messiah to appear, unlike later believers already possessing categories for saintly appearances.
Jewish followers had categories for exalted or disembodied survival until the final resurrection, leaving their claim that Jesus had bodily risen already as a novel development requiring explanation.

conSelections.proposition: Unexpected Marian experiences show that lack of immediate expectation neither distinguishes the Jesus experiences nor establishes that the perceived figure appeared.
Initial followers could sincerely think they saw Jesus, after which apocalyptic Jewish embodiment beliefs could convert those experiences into the claim that God raised the Messiah.

sectionSelections.title: Cumulative fit and historical probability
sectionSelections.rationale: The motion ultimately turns on whether several converging facts can make resurrection plausible despite the methodological difficulty of inferring a singular physical event.

proSelections.proposition: Early Pauline sources are used to organize a cumulative case from Jesus's crucifixion, the unexpected resurrection claim, reported appearances, and Christianity's subsequent spread.
Appearances are only one component of the cumulative case, and the historical evidence is presented as consistent with what would be expected if Jesus rose.

conSelections.proposition: Historians cannot treat an alleged one-time violation of physical law as the most probable explanation merely because a few people reported it.
Historical conclusions compare probabilities, making ordinary misperception more likely than a unique physical exception even if supernatural intervention is abstractly possible.

sectionSelections.title: Christian expansion and the worldwide mission claim
sectionSelections.rationale: Christianity's historical reach matters only if its scale or fulfillment of an attributed mission bears specifically on resurrection rather than merely recording successful belief.

proSelections.proposition: Jesus's singular worldwide worship and divine status are presented as an extraordinary historical anomaly that makes the further extraordinary claim of resurrection more plausible.
The proposed evidence is not popularity alone but the improbable fulfillment of the specific worldwide mission attributed to the risen Jesus.

conSelections.proposition: The number of people convinced that a miracle occurred establishes widespread belief but not the miracle, because movements acquire adherents for nonmiraculous reasons.
The worldwide-mission saying comes through later Gospel authors, religious growth does not indicate truth, and incomplete global conversion undercuts the claimed fulfillment.

sectionSelections.title: Later visions and cross-religious parallels
sectionSelections.rationale: Post-apostolic dreams and visions provide an additional proposed evidential line whose relevance depends on whether they indicate continuing agency or generic religious experience.

proSelections.proposition: Reports of Jesus appearing in dreams and visions across cultures and centuries are offered as additional evidence that he rose and remains active.
The present worldwide pattern of Jesus visions, including reports from people previously unfamiliar with him, is distinguished from dormant ancient cult traditions as evidentially significant.

conSelections.proposition: Dreams do not establish that their objects are real, and analogous dream-appearance traditions in other religions contest the asserted uniqueness of Jesus visions.

Among the proposed facts, appearance reports supply the relevant historical evidence, but testimony from a few witnesses cannot establish an event contrary to consistently observed natural regularities.
